title: Tacoma Attorney Sues USCIS Over H-1B Delay Blocking Work for Detained Immigrants
excerpt: An Olympia nonprofit paid $2,965 for premium processing of its new attorney's H-1B petition. The complaint says USCIS missed its 15-business-day deadline, took no required action for months, and kept the fee.
body:
• A Tacoma immigration attorney and the Olympia nonprofit that hired her sued USCIS on November 13, 2026, alleging the agency missed its premium-processing deadline on her H-1B petition and kept the $2,965 expedite fee, according to KING 5.
  • Glice Nina Esquivel Tripodi Pereira, a Brazilian national and Seattle University law graduate licensed in Washington, was hired to represent detained immigrants but cannot start work without the work authorisation the petition would give her.
  • Premium processing buys a step, not an approval: within 15 business days USCIS must approve, deny, issue a notice of intent to deny, or request more evidence — and an evidence request restarts the 15-day clock when the response arrives, according to the complaint.
  • The suit asks a judge to order USCIS to act within 10 business days and declare the delay unlawful; it does not ask the court to order the petition approved.

An immigration attorney hired to defend detained immigrants cannot start her job, because her own work visa petition is stuck — even though her employer paid USCIS $2,965 to decide it fast. Legal Immigration Services of Olympia and attorney Glice Nina Esquivel Tripodi Pereira filed a federal lawsuit on November 13, 2026, in the US District Court in Tacoma, alleging that US Citizenship and Immigration Services missed a required premium-processing deadline and, months later, has still neither acted on the petition nor refunded the fee, according to KING 5.

Who is affected

"An August 30 email cited in the complaint confirmed the agency had received the response and acknowledged the case had reached "day 21" without a notice being issued."

Esquivel is a Brazilian national and a graduate of Seattle University School of Law, licensed to practise law in Washington, according to KING 5. Legal Immigration Services of Olympia selected her to represent detained immigrants — clients facing urgent hearings and filing deadlines — and budgeted for her position. Without the work authorisation that depends on the H-1B petition, the nonprofit cannot employ her. The delay has strained its existing staff and made it harder to serve those clients, the complaint says, and Esquivel herself faces uncertainty about her ability to remain and work in the United States.

What the rule requires, and what the complaint says happened

Premium processing is USCIS's paid expedite service, requested on Form I-907 alongside the employer's Form I-129 petition. It does not guarantee an approval. What it guarantees, according to the complaint, is a step within 15 business days: USCIS must approve the petition, deny it, issue a notice of intent to deny, or request additional evidence. If the agency requests evidence, a new 15-business-day period begins when it receives the response.

The timeline the complaint lays out is specific. The nonprofit filed its petition on June 26. USCIS requested additional information, and the plaintiffs submitted their response on July 30. An August 30 email cited in the complaint confirmed the agency had received the response and acknowledged the case had reached "day 21" without a notice being issued. The plaintiffs allege that by the time they sued — after follow-up inquiries and a written demand on October 2 — USCIS had still taken none of the required actions and had not refunded the premium-processing fee.

What the lawsuit asks for

The suit names the Department of Homeland Security, USCIS and three agency officials as defendants. It asks a judge to order the agency to take action on the petition within 10 business days, or sooner; to declare the delay unlawful; and to reimburse the plaintiffs' legal fees and costs, according to KING 5. It pointedly does not ask the court to require approval of the petition — only a decision, whichever way it goes. KING 5's report is drawn from the complaint; the government's answer will be filed in the Tacoma court as the case proceeds.

What this means if you have a premium-processing case

The case is a reminder of how the expedite clock actually works for H-1B employers and workers. The 15-business-day count runs from when USCIS receives the petition and fee, it pauses in effect when an evidence request goes out, and it restarts when the response arrives — so a case can be months old and still be measured against a 15-day clock that only started recently. What premium processing promises at each stage is one of the four actions above, not a favourable outcome. When the clock runs out with no action, this lawsuit shows the escalation path employers use: document the missed deadline, make a written demand, and, if the agency still does not move, ask a federal court to compel a decision.
